sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Make the new free-plan account safe before any other mission touches it. Every sign-in uses MFA, everyday work runs as an admin user instead of the root user, two budgets email you at the first sign of real spend, and you know which services the free plan offers. Every other mission stays locked until this one is done and its Verify holds.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Use a new AWS account on the free plan that you created yourself; agents never create accounts or type credentials.
  • The free plan gives $100 in credits at sign-up and lets you earn up to $100 more.
  • It ends after 6 months or when the credits run out, whichever comes first, and the account then closes.
  • The free plan charges nothing unless you upgrade to the Paid plan.
  • After this mission, never sign in as the root user again.
  • Pick one home Region now and use it for every mission.
  • Install AWS CLI version 2.32.0 or later, the first version with the aws login command.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Root user MFA

  • Sign in as the root user, choose your account name on the right side of the navigation bar, and choose Security credentials.
  • In the Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) section, choose Assign MFA device, name the device, choose Authenticator app, and finish the wizard with two consecutive codes from the app.
  • Keep a secure backup of the QR code or secret key, because losing the only MFA device locks the root user out until AWS customer service removes it.

Billing access for IAM users

  • Still signed in as the root user, open the Account page of the Billing and Cost Management console.
  • Under IAM user and role access to Billing information, choose Edit, select Activate IAM access, and choose Update.
  • Without this setting, IAM users cannot open billing pages such as Budgets, Credits, Billing preferences and Cost Explorer, even with admin permissions, and only the root user can turn it on.

Admin user with MFA

  • In the IAM console, create a user named ccp-admin with console access.
  • Attach the AdministratorAccess and SignInLocalDevelopmentAccess managed policies to it.
  • Note the account sign-in URL that IAM shows for the new user.
  • In the IAM console, choose Users, choose ccp-admin, open the Security Credentials tab, choose Assign MFA device under Multi-factor authentication (MFA), and finish the wizard as for the root user.
  • Sign out of the root user, and sign in at that URL as ccp-admin for everything that follows.
  • If the IAM console will not create an IAM user with console access, for example because the account uses the new AWS experience with projects and AWS Settings, stop: do not continue this or any later mission, and never work around it as the root user or with IAM Identity Center.

CLI sign-in without access keys

  • Run aws login --profile ccp-admin, enter your home Region when the CLI asks for one, and finish the sign-in as ccp-admin in the browser.
  • Check it with aws sts get-caller-identity --profile ccp-admin, which prints an ARN ending in user/ccp-admin.
  • The CLI refreshes these short-term credentials for up to 12 hours, and running aws login --profile ccp-admin again starts a new session.

Two budgets with credits excluded

  • In the Billing and Cost Management console, choose Budgets, then Create budget, then Use a template (simplified).
  • Create the Zero spend budget template with your email as the recipient, so spending beyond the Free Tier limits sends an email.
  • Create the Monthly cost budget template with a budget amount of $5 and the same recipient.
  • In each budget, choose Custom under Template settings, then under Budget scope choose Add filter and add a Charge type filter that leaves out Credit, so each budget tracks the usage that the credits pay for.
  • Under Advanced options in the same section, choose Use unblended costs, because net unblended and net amortized costs subtract the credits again.
  • Set the $5 budget's alerts to 50%, 80% and 100% of actual cost and 100% of forecasted cost.
  • Open the verification email that AWS Budgets sends and choose its link while signed in to this account, because budget alerts reach only verified recipients.
  • If a budget's detail page shows your address as Pending, check your spam folder or choose Resend verification, because the link expires 12 hours after it is sent.
  • One verification covers every budget in this account that uses the same address.
  • Wait for no alert email: an actual-cost alert is sent only when a threshold is first reached, and forecast alerts need about 5 weeks of usage data.

Free Tier usage alerts

  • In the Billing console, under Preferences, choose Billing preferences.
  • For Alert preferences, choose Edit, make sure Receive AWS Free Tier alerts is selected, check the email address that receives them, and choose Update.
  • These emails arrive when a service passes 85 percent of its Free Tier limit.
  • On the free plan, AWS also emails you about your credit balance and when the plan nears its end.

Home Region

  • Choose the Region closest to you and use it in the console's Region selector for every mission.
  • The ccp-admin CLI profile already uses it, because aws login asked for it.

Plan status

  • Write down your plan, your credit balance and the date the free plan ends or its days remaining, which the console home page and the Billing and Cost Management console home show.
  • For each service a later mission uses, mark on the Plan status form below the steps whether the free plan offers it.
  • The AWS Free Tier page marks some services, such as Amazon EC2, Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB, as available on both plans, but it does not list every service.
  • Leave a service you cannot confirm unticked, because the form counts an unticked service as not offered until you confirm it.
  • A mission that needs a service the plan lacks stays locked.

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • The Budgets page lists both budgets, and each budget's detail page shows your email as a recipient with the status Active, not Pending.
  • Each budget's scope has a Charge type filter that leaves out Credit, and each budget uses unblended costs.
  • The root user's security credentials and the ccp-admin user's both show an assigned MFA device.
  • Signed in as ccp-admin, you can open the Budgets page and the Billing preferences page.
  • aws sts get-caller-identity --profile ccp-admin prints the ccp-admin user's ARN, not the root user's.
  • The Plan status form below the steps shows the day you saved your plan, credit balance and end date, with a tick for every service the free plan offers.

sections.title: Never do
sections.html:
Never do

  • Never upgrade the account to the Paid plan.
  • Never enable IAM Identity Center or create or join an AWS organization, because on a free-plan account joining AWS Organizations upgrades it to the Paid plan and the credits expire at once.
  • Never set up an AWS Control Tower landing zone or join the AWS Partner Network, because each of these also upgrades a free-plan account to the Paid plan.
  • Never accept an agreement in AWS Artifact, such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA), because designating the account as HIPAA or SEC compliant also upgrades a free-plan account to the Paid plan.
  • Never sign a Professional Services contract or an Enterprise Agreement with AWS, or buy an AWS Skill Builder Team subscription, on this account, because each of these upgrades it too.
  • Never create access keys, for the root user or for ccp-admin, because aws login gives the CLI short-term credentials.
  • Never create NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses or unattached Elastic IPs.
  • Never create RDS or Aurora databases, EKS clusters, Redshift, OpenSearch or SageMaker endpoints.
  • Never turn on Shield Advanced or order Direct Connect.
  • Never register Route 53 domains or create hosted zones.
  • Never buy Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and never subscribe to Marketplace products.

missions.title: Host this site on S3 and CloudFront
canUseCredits: CloudFront requests and data transfer out

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Serve this study site from a private S3 bucket that only CloudFront can read, so you can read every note on your phone.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds.
  • Your Plan status form says the free plan offers Amazon S3, Amazon CloudFront and AWS CloudFormation; if any of them is unticked, stop here and keep using pnpm preview on the Mac.
  • Your terminal is signed in with aws login --profile ccp-admin.
  • The repo has no uncommitted changes and pnpm verify passes, because the deploy command refuses to run otherwise.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Create the hosting stack

aws cloudformation deploy --template-file infra/site.yaml --stack-name ccp-study-site --profile ccp-admin
  • The stack creates a private bucket with all four Block Public Access settings on, a CloudFront distribution that reads the bucket through origin access control (OAC), and a response headers policy with the site's Content-Security-Policy.
  • With OAC, CloudFront signs every request it sends to the bucket, and the bucket policy lets the CloudFront service read objects only on behalf of this distribution.
  • The command creates a change set, runs it, and returns once CloudFormation has run it.
  • Running it again later updates the same stack, and with an unchanged template it reports no changes and still exits with success.

Upload the site

pnpm site:deploy
  • The command runs pnpm verify, uploads the build to the bucket, invalidates the entry files, removes chunks that no recent build uses, and prints the site URL.

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • Open the printed SiteUrl on your phone and check that Home lists the 13 modules.
  • Check that the bucket refuses a direct read: the commands below print 403 and then AccessDenied.
BUCKET=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name ccp-study-site --profile ccp-admin --query "Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey=='BucketName'].OutputValue" --output text)
REGION=$(aws configure get region --profile ccp-admin)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "https://$BUCKET.s3.$REGION.amazonaws.com/index.html"
curl -s "https://$BUCKET.s3.$REGION.amazonaws.com/index.html" | grep -o AccessDenied
  • If the direct S3 address returns the page instead, stop and check the bucket's Block Public Access settings and bucket policy before you go on.

sections.title: Keep it running
sections.html:
Keep it running

  • The bucket and the distribution carry the tag ccp:keep=site, so a Tag Editor search for that tag across all Regions lists both, and the cleanup of later missions leaves them alone.
  • The next day, open Cost Explorer with daily costs grouped by service, and check that Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront stay within a few cents.
  • Run pnpm site:deploy again whenever you want to publish a new build.
  • This mission has no cleanup step and no time limit, because the site stays up.
  • The site lives only as long as the account: the free plan ends after 6 months or when the credits run out, and the account then closes.

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Take one small web server on Amazon EC2 from launch to termination, and see what each lifecycle step keeps and what it throws away. You serve a one-line page from user data, open a browser shell with EC2 Instance Connect and no key pair, watch the public IPv4 address change across a stop and start, and see which volumes outlive the instance.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds, and your Plan status form says the free plan offers Amazon EC2 and Amazon VPC; if either is unticked, stop here.
  • Sign in to the console as ccp-admin, never as the root user, and work only in the home Region you picked in Mission 0.
  • Run every CLI command with --profile ccp-admin.
  • Tag every resource you can with ccp:mission=mission-02, that is the key ccp:mission and the value mission-02.
  • Three things can use credits: the instance's running hours, its public IPv4 address, and the storage of both EBS volumes until they are deleted.
  • A public IPv4 address is charged by the hour whether it is in use or idle.
  • On the free plan these charges count against your credits, and nothing is billed to you unless you upgrade to the Paid plan.
  • Finish Cleanup within 2 hours of pressing Start.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Launch one instance with a page in its user data

  • In the EC2 console, choose Launch instance, name it ccp-m02-web, and under Add additional tags add ccp:mission=mission-02 for the instance, volumes and network interfaces.
  • Pick the Amazon Linux 2023 AMI marked Free tier eligible from Quick Start; its standard edition comes with EC2 Instance Connect installed, which is why you can skip the key pair.
  • Choose t3.micro, which the EC2 free tier page lists for accounts created on or after July 15, 2025, and check that the console marks it Free tier eligible.
  • Under Key pair (login), choose to proceed without a key pair.
  • Under Network settings, keep the default VPC, its default subnet and Auto-assign public IP on Enable, the default in a default subnet.
  • Choose Edit, let the wizard create a new security group, and swap its default SSH rule from anywhere for these two inbound rules:
    • SSH on port 22 from the prefix list com.amazonaws.REGION.ec2-instance-connect, with your Region code for REGION, because a console connection arrives from the EC2 Instance Connect service, not from your Mac.
    • HTTP on port 80 from your own public IPv4 address with the /32 suffix.
  • If the wizard will not take the prefix list, give SSH your /32 address for now and switch it to the prefix list in the group's inbound rules before you connect.
  • Under Configure storage, add one extra 1 GiB gp3 volume and leave its Delete on termination at the console default, which is No for a data volume added at launch.
  • Under Advanced details, paste this into User data; the first line marks it as cloud-init directives.
#cloud-config
packages:
  - httpd
runcmd:
  - [ sh, -c, "echo 'Mission 2 web page is up' > /var/www/html/index.html" ]
  - systemctl start httpd
  - systemctl enable httpd
  • Launch exactly 1 instance, then add ccp:mission=mission-02 to the new security group as well, because the wizard did not tag it.
  • Wait for running and passed status checks, then a few minutes more: user data runs as root during the first boot only, and it slows that boot down.

Connect with EC2 Instance Connect

  • Select the instance, choose Connect, open the EC2 Instance Connect tab, keep Connect using a Public IP and the user ec2-user, and choose Connect.
  • A browser terminal opens, because the service pushed a public key to the instance that lasts only 60 seconds.
  • Check the page and the end of the user data log, then close the tab.
curl -s http://localhost/
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/cloud-init-output.log

Stop and start once

  • Write down the public and private IPv4 addresses, then choose Instance state, Stop instance.
  • While it is stopped, the instance bills nothing, but its EBS volumes still bill for storage.
  • Choose Instance state, Start instance, and compare: the stop released the public IPv4 address and the start gave a new one, while the private address stayed.
  • Each start bills at least one minute, so do this once.
  • The page still loads, because httpd is enabled at boot even though user data does not run again.

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • From your Mac, load the page over plain http at the new address and see Mission 2 web page is up.
curl -s http://PUBLIC_IPV4_ADDRESS/
  • Use the instance's current public IPv4 address or public DNS name; if the request hangs, check the HTTP rule against your Mac's current address.
  • On the instance's Storage tab, the Block devices table shows Delete on termination as Yes for the root volume and No for the 1 GiB volume.

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.html:
Cleanup

  • Terminate the instance first, because a security group still tied to an instance and a volume still attached to one cannot be deleted: choose Instance state, Terminate (delete) instance, and confirm; instance charges stop at shutting-down.
  • In Volumes, confirm that the root volume is gone, since it was set to delete on termination.
  • Delete any EBS volume left available after termination: the 1 GiB gp3 volume now shows Available, so choose Actions, Delete volume, and type delete, because a preserved volume bills until deleted.
  • Delete the launch-wizard security group created for ccp-m02-web, and never the VPC's default group.
  • The terminated instance stays listed for a short while and then vanishes on its own; the docs give no exact time and suggest contacting Support only after several hours.
  • In Tag Editor, select every Region and All resource types, search for the tag key ccp:mission, and see 0 results.

sections.title: Usage check
sections.html:
Usage check

  • On the next study day, open Cost Explorer with daily granularity, grouped by Service.
  • Cost Explorer splits Amazon EC2 into EC2 - Instances and EC2 - Other, and EBS storage lands in EC2 - Other.
  • Compare both of those and Amazon VPC, whose pricing page lists the public IPv4 charge, with the day before Start, not with zero; if one is still higher, go back to Cleanup.
  • Note your remaining credit balance and record it with the usage button on this page.

sections.title: Never do
sections.html:
Never do

  • Never upgrade the account to the Paid plan, and never change the Support plan.
  • Never create NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses or unattached Elastic IPs, and never give this instance an Elastic IP.
  • Never create RDS or Aurora databases, EKS clusters, Redshift, OpenSearch or SageMaker endpoints.
  • Never turn on Shield Advanced, order Direct Connect, register Route 53 domains or create hosted zones.
  • Never buy Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and never subscribe to Marketplace products.
  • Never create access keys, for the root user or for ccp-admin.
  • Never enable IAM Identity Center or create or join an AWS organization, because on a free-plan account creating an organization upgrades it to the Paid plan and the credits expire at once.
  • Never set up an AWS Control Tower landing zone or join the AWS Partner Network, because each of these upgrades a free-plan account.
  • Never accept an agreement in AWS Artifact, such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA), because designating the account as HIPAA compliant upgrades it.
  • Never sign a Professional Services contract or an Enterprise Agreement, or buy an AWS Skill Builder Team subscription, because each of these upgrades it too.
  • Never launch a second instance or one not marked Free tier eligible, and never open SSH or HTTP to 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Never leave the instance stopped instead of terminated, because its volumes keep billing.

missions.title: An S3 upload that logs a receipt through Lambda
canUseCredits: Lambda invocations beyond the free usage

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

See event-driven serverless compute work end to end: dropping one file into a new private bucket runs a Lambda function, and the function writes a one-line receipt with the file's key to CloudWatch Logs. You never start or stop a server, and the only trace the function leaves is that log line.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds, and your Plan status form says the free plan offers Amazon S3, AWS Lambda and Amazon CloudWatch Logs; if one is unticked, stop here.
  • Sign in to the console as ccp-admin, never as the root user.
  • Work in the home Region you picked in Mission 0, in every console page and every command.
  • Run every CLI command with --profile ccp-admin, after aws login --profile ccp-admin if your session has expired.
  • Tag every resource that accepts tags with the key ccp:mission and the value mission-03, written here as ccp:mission=mission-03.
  • What can use credits: Lambda invocations beyond the monthly free usage of one million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds, S3 storage and requests, and log storage, because Lambda logs carry the standard CloudWatch Logs charges.
  • Note the time when you press Start, and finish the Cleanup within 2 hours of it.
  • Pick a function name, here ccp-receipt, and a globally unique bucket name in lower case, here ccp-receipts-<your initials>-<today's date>.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Create the bucket

  • In the S3 console, open General purpose buckets, choose Create bucket, keep the bucket type General purpose, and enter your bucket name.
  • Leave the other options at their defaults, but check that all four Block Public Access settings are on, turn on any that is off, and create the bucket.
  • Open the bucket, choose the Properties tab, and add the tag ccp:mission=mission-03 in its Tags section.
  • New buckets have versioning turned off, which keeps the later emptying to one command.

Create the function with the default role

  • In the Lambda console, choose Create function, then Author from scratch, name it ccp-receipt, and choose a current Python runtime such as Python 3.14.
  • Leave the execution role at its default, so the console creates a new role that can only write logs to CloudWatch Logs.
  • Under Advanced settings, select Enable tags, add the tag ccp:mission=mission-03, and choose Create function.
  • In the Code tab, replace the starter code with the handler below and choose Deploy.
import urllib.parse

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    for record in event["Records"]:
        key = urllib.parse.unquote_plus(record["s3"]["object"]["key"])
        print(f"receipt {key}")
  • The handler only prints; it never calls S3, so it cannot write back to the bucket and start a loop.

Tag the execution role

  • In the IAM console, choose Roles and search for ccp-receipt-role, because the console names the new role after the function and adds a short random suffix.
  • Write down that role name and every policy listed on its Permissions tab, because the Cleanup needs both.
  • On the role's Tags tab, add the tag ccp:mission=mission-03 and save.
  • If that list holds a customer managed policy, open it under Policies, choose its Tags tab and Manage tags, add the same tag, and save.
  • Add no other policy to the role: basic logging is all this function needs.

Add the S3 trigger

  • In the function's Function overview, choose Add trigger, select S3, and pick your bucket.
  • Keep the event type at All object create events.
  • Tick the Recursive invocation box only after you have checked that the function never writes to this bucket, then choose Add.

Upload one small test object

echo "one receipt" > receipt-test.txt
aws s3 cp receipt-test.txt s3://YOUR-BUCKET/receipt-test.txt --profile ccp-admin
  • Upload this one small file and nothing else.

Tag the log group and shorten its retention

  • Lambda sends the function's logs to the log group /aws/lambda/ccp-receipt, so do this step after the upload, once that log group is listed in the CloudWatch console.
  • Tag it with the CLI, which takes the log group ARN without any trailing :*.
REGION=$(aws configure get region --profile ccp-admin)
ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text --profile ccp-admin)
aws logs tag-resource --resource-arn "arn:aws:logs:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:log-group:/aws/lambda/ccp-receipt" --tags ccp:mission=mission-03 --profile ccp-admin
  • Optionally, keep its log events for 1 day instead of the default of never expiring.
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/lambda/ccp-receipt --retention-in-days 1 --profile ccp-admin

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • In the CloudWatch console, open the log group /aws/lambda/ccp-receipt, choose the newest log stream, and find the line receipt receipt-test.txt.
  • The line can take 5 to 10 minutes to appear after the upload.
  • From the terminal, the command below prints the same line.
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/lambda/ccp-receipt --filter-pattern receipt --query "events[].message" --output text --profile ccp-admin
  • The log stream holds exactly one receipt line, which shows the function ran once per upload and did not loop.

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.html:
Cleanup

  • First remove the trigger: on the function's Configuration tab, choose Triggers, select the S3 trigger, and choose Delete.
  • Delete the function: on the Lambda Functions page, select ccp-receipt, choose Actions, then Delete, and type confirm.
  • Delete the /aws/lambda/<function> log group, here /aws/lambda/ccp-receipt, which also removes every log event in it.
aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name /aws/lambda/ccp-receipt --profile ccp-admin
  • Delete the execution role and its policy: in the IAM console, delete the role you wrote down, which detaches its managed policies but does not delete them.
  • Then, under Policies, delete any customer managed policy you wrote down for that role, and leave AWS managed policies such as AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole in place.
  • Empty the bucket, then delete it.
aws s3 rm s3://YOUR-BUCKET --recursive --profile ccp-admin
aws s3 rb s3://YOUR-BUCKET --profile ccp-admin
  • Delete the local receipt-test.txt file.
  • Open Tag Editor, select every Region in its Regions list, choose All resource types, search for the tag key ccp:mission in all Regions, and check that the search returns 0 results.

sections.title: Usage check
sections.html:
Usage check

  • On the next study day, open Cost Explorer with daily granularity, grouped by Service.
  • Cost Explorer counts days in UTC, so find the bar for the day before Start and the latest full day after Cleanup.
  • Check that AWS Lambda, Amazon S3 and CloudWatch on that latest day are back to their level on the day before Start, comparing with that day and not with zero, because Mission 1 keeps S3 billing every day.
  • If one is still higher, go back to Cleanup and look for a leftover bucket, function or log group.
  • Then note the remaining credit balance, which this page records with the usage button.

sections.title: Never do
sections.html:
Never do

  • Never upgrade to the Paid plan or change the Support plan.
  • Never create NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses or unattached Elastic IPs.
  • Never create RDS or Aurora databases, EKS clusters, Redshift, OpenSearch or SageMaker endpoints.
  • Never turn on Shield Advanced or order Direct Connect.
  • Never register Route 53 domains or create hosted zones.
  • Never buy Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and never subscribe to Marketplace products.
  • Never create access keys, least of all root access keys.
  • Never enable IAM Identity Center or create or join an organization, because on a free-plan account creating an organization moves it to the Paid plan and its credits expire at once.
  • Never create a Control Tower landing zone, become an AWS Partner Network member, accept an AWS Artifact agreement such as the BAA, sign a Professional Services contract or Enterprise Agreement, or buy an AWS Skill Builder Team subscription, because each of these upgrades a free-plan account.
  • Never let the function write to the bucket that triggers it, never add S3 permissions to its role, and never change its recursive loop detection to Allow recursive loops.
  • Never turn off Block Public Access on the bucket.
  • Never upload more than the one small test object.

missions.title: A DynamoDB loyalty table on demand

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Give the cafe a loyalty table in Amazon DynamoDB that bills per request, store a few members in it, and fetch one member back by its key. You see a fully managed NoSQL table do its job with no servers and no capacity to plan, then you delete it the same day.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds.
  • Your Plan status form says the free plan offers Amazon DynamoDB; if it is unticked, stop here.
  • Sign in to the console as ccp-admin, never as the root user.
  • Work in the home Region you chose in Mission 0, and check the console's Region selector shows it.
  • Run every CLI command with --profile ccp-admin, after aws login --profile ccp-admin if your session has expired.
  • Tag every taggable resource ccp:mission=mission-04, that is the tag key ccp:mission with the value mission-04.
  • Here the table is the only resource, and DynamoDB copies a table's tags onto any index it has.
  • Only on-demand read and write requests and the table's storage can use credits in this mission, and a few tiny items should come to about $0.
  • Write down the date and time you begin as Start, and finish Cleanup within 2 hours of Start.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Create the table on demand

  • Open the DynamoDB console, choose Tables, then Create table.
  • Name the table ccp-loyalty and set the partition key to MemberId of type String, with no sort key.
  • Under Table settings, choose Customize settings instead of Default settings.
  • The docs disagree on what Default settings gives you: one page calls on-demand the default throughput option, while the console auto scaling page says a table made with the defaults gets auto scaling, which belongs to provisioned capacity.
  • So pick the mode yourself: keep DynamoDB Standard as the table class, and under Read/write capacity settings choose On-demand.
  • In the Tags section, choose Add new tag and enter the key ccp:mission with the value mission-04.
  • Leave deletion protection off and add no indexes, then choose Create table and wait until the status reads ACTIVE.
  • To do the same from the CLI instead, run the command below, where PAY_PER_REQUEST is the CLI name for on-demand.
aws dynamodb create-table \
  --table-name ccp-loyalty \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=MemberId,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=MemberId,KeyType=HASH \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --table-class STANDARD \
  --tags Key=ccp:mission,Value=mission-04 \
  --profile ccp-admin

Check the mode and the tag

aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name ccp-loyalty --profile ccp-admin \
  --query "Table.[TableStatus,BillingModeSummary.BillingMode,ProvisionedThroughput]"
ARN=$(aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name ccp-loyalty --profile ccp-admin --query Table.TableArn --output text)
aws dynamodb list-tags-of-resource --resource-arn "$ARN" --profile ccp-admin
  • The first command prints ACTIVE, PAY_PER_REQUEST and read and write capacity units of 0, which is how an on-demand table describes itself.
  • The second prints the ccp:mission tag with the value mission-04.
  • If the mode shows PROVISIONED, switch it at once with aws dynamodb update-table --table-name ccp-loyalty --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST --profile ccp-admin.

Put a few members

aws dynamodb put-item --table-name ccp-loyalty --profile ccp-admin \
  --item '{"MemberId": {"S": "m-001"}, "Name": {"S": "Ana"}, "Points": {"N": "120"}}'
aws dynamodb put-item --table-name ccp-loyalty --profile ccp-admin \
  --item '{"MemberId": {"S": "m-002"}, "Name": {"S": "Ben"}, "Points": {"N": "45"}}'
aws dynamodb put-item --table-name ccp-loyalty --profile ccp-admin \
  --item '{"MemberId": {"S": "m-003"}, "Name": {"S": "Chloe"}, "Points": {"N": "310"}}'
  • In the console you can add the same items from Explore table items with Create item, adding Name as a String and Points as a Number.
  • Each item stays far below 1 KB, the size one write request unit covers.

Query one member by key

aws dynamodb query --table-name ccp-loyalty --profile ccp-admin \
  --key-condition-expression "MemberId = :id" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":id": {"S": "m-002"}}'
  • A query needs an exact value for the partition key, and it returns every item that carries that value.
  • In the console, open Explore table items, keep Query selected, enter m-002 as the partition key and choose Run.

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • The query prints "Count": 1 and one item whose MemberId is m-002, with Name set to Ben and Points set to 45.
  • The console query for m-002 lists that same single item under Items returned.
  • describe-table showed PAY_PER_REQUEST, and list-tags-of-resource showed ccp:mission with the value mission-04.

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.html:
Cleanup

  • This mission has no leftovers in its frontmatter, so start with the table itself.
  • Delete the table in the console by ticking ccp-loyalty under Tables and choosing Delete, or run the command below.
aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name ccp-loyalty --profile ccp-admin
aws dynamodb list-tables --profile ccp-admin
  • The table passes through DELETING, and a deleted table cannot be brought back.
  • Run list-tables again until ccp-loyalty no longer appears in the list of table names it prints.
  • Open Tag Editor, select every Region and All resource types, search for the tag key ccp:mission, and check that it returns 0 results.

sections.title: Usage check
sections.html:
Usage check

  • On the next study day, open Cost Explorer, choose Daily granularity, group by Service, and add a Charge type filter set to Usage so credits do not hide the usage.
  • Cost Explorer counts days in UTC, so find the bar for the day before Start and the latest full day after Cleanup.
  • Check that Amazon DynamoDB on that latest day is back to its level from the day before Start, comparing with that day and not with zero.
  • Any cost on the day of Start should be a fraction of a cent, because the pricing page bills on-demand requests per million.
  • Note the remaining credit balance from the Billing and Cost Management console home, and record it with the usage button on this page.

sections.title: Never do
sections.html:
Never do

  • Never upgrade the account to the Paid plan, and never change the Support plan.
  • Never turn on point-in-time recovery or take an on-demand backup, even though the getting-started tutorial suggests point-in-time recovery, because the pricing page charges both by table size.
  • Never enable DynamoDB Streams, add a global table replica, create a DAX cluster, or export the table to S3, because each one carries its own charge on the pricing page.
  • Never switch the table to provisioned capacity or to the Standard-IA table class, and never turn on deletion protection, because it would block Cleanup.
  • Never enable IAM Identity Center or create or join an AWS organization, because on a free-plan account that upgrades it to the Paid plan and the credits expire at once.
  • Never set up an AWS Control Tower landing zone or join the AWS Partner Network, because each of these upgrades a free-plan account too.
  • Never accept an agreement in AWS Artifact, such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA), because marking the account as HIPAA or SEC compliant upgrades it as well.
  • Never sign a Professional Services contract or an Enterprise Agreement with AWS, or buy an AWS Skill Builder Team subscription, on this account.
  • Never create access keys, for the root user or for ccp-admin, because aws login gives the CLI short-term credentials.
  • Never create NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses or unattached Elastic IPs.
  • Never create RDS or Aurora databases, EKS clusters, Redshift, OpenSearch or SageMaker endpoints.
  • Never turn on Shield Advanced or order Direct Connect.
  • Never register Route 53 domains or create hosted zones.
  • Never buy Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and never subscribe to Marketplace products.

missions.title: A least-privilege role, tested and traced

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Build one role that can do exactly one thing, prove with the IAM policy simulator that it can do that thing and nothing next to it, and then find your own setup calls in CloudTrail. The role can read objects under one prefix of one bucket, and every other combination in the matrix below must come back denied.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds.
  • Your Plan status form says the free plan offers AWS Identity and Access Management and AWS CloudTrail; if either is unticked, stop here.
  • Sign in to the console as ccp-admin, never as the root user.
  • Keep the console in the home Region you chose in Mission 0, except for the Event history step, which says why it switches Region.
  • Sign the terminal in with aws login --profile ccp-admin, and run every command below with --profile ccp-admin.
  • Tag every taggable resource with the key ccp:mission and the value mission-05, written ccp:mission=mission-05.
  • What can use credits: nothing, because IAM is offered at no extra charge and CloudTrail does not charge for viewing Event history.
  • Start the mission on this page before your first command, and finish Cleanup within 2 hours of Start.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Write the two policy documents

mkdir -p ~/ccp-m05 && cd ~/ccp-m05
ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --profile ccp-admin --query Account --output text)
cat > trust.json <<EOF
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT}:root" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
    "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true" } }
  }]
}
EOF
cat > reader.json <<EOF
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-demo/reports/*"
  }]
}
EOF
  • The trust policy names only this account as the principal, and only with MFA, so no other account and no AWS service can take the role.
  • Naming the account is not enough on its own: an identity in it also needs its own permission to call sts:AssumeRole on the role.
  • The permissions policy grants one action on one resource ARN, with no * in any action.
  • Neither bucket in this mission has to exist, because the simulator never sends a request to Amazon S3.

Create the customer managed policy

POLICY_ARN=$(aws iam create-policy --profile ccp-admin --policy-name ccp-m05-read-reports \
  --policy-document file://reader.json --tags Key=ccp:mission,Value=mission-05 \
  --query Policy.Arn --output text)
echo "$POLICY_ARN"
  • A customer managed policy lives in your account and can be attached to roles, users and groups, which is the step from broad AWS managed policies toward least privilege.

Create the role and attach the policy

aws iam create-role --profile ccp-admin --role-name ccp-m05-reader \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json --tags Key=ccp:mission,Value=mission-05
aws iam attach-role-policy --profile ccp-admin --role-name ccp-m05-reader --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN"
  • If a tag is malformed, create-role fails as a whole and creates nothing.

Run the allow and deny matrix

Action Resource Expected
s3:GetObject arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-demo/reports/jan.csv allowed
s3:PutObject arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-demo/reports/jan.csv denied
s3:GetObject arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-demo/private/jan.csv denied
s3:PutObject arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-demo/private/jan.csv denied
s3:GetObject arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-other/reports/jan.csv denied
s3:PutObject arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-other/reports/jan.csv denied
  • In the IAM console, choose Policy simulator in the navigation pane, not the old standalone simulator site, which AWS no longer maintains.
  • In Principal mode, pick the role ccp-m05-reader, add s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject, enter the three resource ARNs from the table, and run the simulation.
  • Every denied row should read implicitly denied, because nothing allows it and IAM refuses anything that no policy allows.
  • Run the same matrix from the terminal as a second witness.
aws iam simulate-principal-policy --profile ccp-admin \
  --policy-source-arn "arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT}:role/ccp-m05-reader" \
  --action-names s3:GetObject s3:PutObject \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-demo/reports/jan.csv arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-demo/private/jan.csv arn:aws:s3:::ccp-m05-other/reports/jan.csv \
  --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName, ResourceSpecificResults[].[EvalResourceName, EvalResourceDecision]]"
  • The command pairs each action with each ARN, and each pair reports allowed, implicitDeny or explicitDeny.

Find your calls in Event history

  • Open the CloudTrail console and switch the Region selector to US East (N. Virginia), because CloudTrail records IAM events in us-east-1 whatever your home Region is.
  • Choose Event history, pick the User name lookup attribute, enter ccp-admin, and set the time range to start just before Start.
  • Event history needs no trail: it is on by default and keeps 90 days of management events for each Region.
  • It takes one attribute filter at a time, so the user name replaces the default read-only filter.
  • Open the CreateRole event and scroll to Event record to see the JSON that CloudTrail kept.
  • If a call is not listed yet, refresh the page a little later.

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • The console simulator shows s3:GetObject on ccp-m05-demo/reports/jan.csv as allowed and the other five rows of the matrix as implicitly denied.
  • The terminal simulation prints allowed for that same pair and implicitDeny for the other five, so every row matches the Expected column, including the denied ones.
  • Event history in us-east-1, filtered by the user name ccp-admin, lists CreatePolicy, CreateRole and AttachRolePolicy from this session.

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.html:
Cleanup

  • Detach its customer managed policy from the role; the first two lines rebuild its ARN, so the commands also work in a new terminal.
ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --profile ccp-admin --query Account --output text)
POLICY_ARN="arn:aws:iam::${ACCOUNT}:policy/ccp-m05-read-reports"
aws iam detach-role-policy --profile ccp-admin --role-name ccp-m05-reader --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN"
  • Delete its customer managed policy.
aws iam delete-policy --profile ccp-admin --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN"
  • Delete the role.
aws iam delete-role --profile ccp-admin --role-name ccp-m05-reader
  • Prove both are gone by name: each command below prints [].
aws iam list-roles --profile ccp-admin --query "Roles[?RoleName=='ccp-m05-reader']"
aws iam list-policies --profile ccp-admin --scope Local --query "Policies[?PolicyName=='ccp-m05-read-reports']"

missions.title: A CloudWatch alarm that emails on Lambda errors
canUseCredits: the alarm beyond the free alarms
SNS email deliveries beyond the free usage

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Watch one Lambda error travel all the way to your inbox. A throwaway function fails when you ask it to, one CloudWatch alarm watches its Errors metric, and one SNS topic emails you when that alarm fires.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds.
  • Your Plan status form says the free plan offers Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon SNS, AWS Lambda and Amazon CloudWatch Logs; if any of them is unticked, stop here.
  • Sign in to the console as ccp-admin, never as the root user.
  • Set the console's Region selector to the home Region you picked in Mission 0.
  • Your terminal is signed in with aws login --profile ccp-admin, and every CLI command below passes --profile ccp-admin, so it runs in that same home Region.
  • Tag every resource that takes tags with the key ccp:mission and the value mission-06, written in this mission as ccp:mission=mission-06.
  • What can use credits: the alarm beyond the free alarms, SNS requests and email deliveries, the Lambda invocations and the log storage.
  • The free tier on the CloudWatch pricing page covers 10 alarm metrics, and only standard-resolution alarms count toward it.
  • Write down the time you begin; that is Start, and the Cleanup must be done within 2 hours of Start.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Create the function

  • In the Lambda console, choose Create function, then Author from scratch, and name it ccp-m06-fail.
  • Pick the Python 3.14 runtime and leave the permissions on the default, so Lambda makes a new execution role whose policy only lets the function write logs.
  • Expand Advanced settings, select Enable tags, add the tag ccp:mission=mission-06, and choose Create function.
  • On the Code tab, replace the starter code with the handler below and choose Deploy.
def lambda_handler(event, context):
    if event.get("fail"):
        raise RuntimeError("mission-06 forced error")
    return {"ok": True}
  • The handler returns normally unless the event carries "fail": true, and then it throws, which Lambda counts as one function error in the Errors metric.

Create the topic and confirm the email

  • In the SNS console, choose Topics, then Create topic.
  • Choose the Standard type, because email endpoints can subscribe only to standard topics, and name it ccp-m06-alarm; neither the type nor the name can change later.
  • Under Tags, add ccp:mission=mission-06, create the topic, and copy its ARN.
  • Choose Subscriptions, then Create subscription, pick the topic's ARN, choose the Email protocol, enter your own address as the endpoint, and create it.
  • Open the email that arrives from AWS Notifications and choose Confirm subscription, and the subscription then reads Confirmed in the console.
  • Confirm it right away, because a pending subscription cannot be deleted by hand and SNS only removes it after 48 hours.

Create the alarm

  • Paste the topic ARN into the first line below, then run the commands.
TOPIC_ARN="paste-the-topic-arn-here"
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --profile ccp-admin \
  --alarm-name ccp-m06-errors \
  --namespace AWS/Lambda --metric-name Errors \
  --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=ccp-m06-fail \
  --statistic Sum --period 60 \
  --evaluation-periods 1 --datapoints-to-alarm 1 \
  --threshold 1 --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold \
  --treat-missing-data notBreaching \
  --alarm-actions "$TOPIC_ARN" \
  --tags Key=ccp:mission,Value=mission-06
  • The alarm adds up the function's errors in each 1-minute period and goes to ALARM when a single period holds 1 error or more.
  • A 60-second period keeps it a standard-resolution alarm, while 10, 20 or 30 seconds would turn it into a high-resolution alarm with a higher charge.
  • Lambda sends metrics when an invocation finishes, so treating the empty minutes between runs as not breaching keeps the alarm in OK, where the default would leave it in INSUFFICIENT_DATA.

Force an error

  • In the Lambda console, open ccp-m06-fail and choose the Test tab.
  • Create a new event named fail, keep Private under the event sharing settings, set its JSON to the line below, save it, and choose Test.
{ "fail": true }
  • The console invokes the function synchronously, and you expand Details under Execution result to review the run.
  • Keep the event private, because Lambda stores shareable test events in an EventBridge schema registry that stays behind when the function is deleted.

Tag the log group, the role and its policy

  • After that first run, tag the log group /aws/lambda/ccp-m06-fail and the execution role, which the console named ccp-m06-fail-role- plus a random suffix.
ACCOUNT=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --profile ccp-admin --query Account --output text)
REGION=$(aws configure get region --profile ccp-admin)
aws logs tag-resource --profile ccp-admin \
  --resource-arn "arn:aws:logs:$REGION:$ACCOUNT:log-group:/aws/lambda/ccp-m06-fail" \
  --tags ccp:mission=mission-06
ROLE=$(aws iam list-roles --profile ccp-admin --query "Roles[?starts_with(RoleName, 'ccp-m06-fail-role-')].RoleName" --output text)
echo "$ROLE"
aws iam tag-role --profile ccp-admin --role-name "$ROLE" --tags Key=ccp:mission,Value=mission-06
aws iam list-attached-role-policies --profile ccp-admin --role-name "$ROLE" --query "AttachedPolicies[].PolicyArn" --output text
  • If echo prints anything but one role name, skip the last two commands, tag the role on its page in the IAM console, and read the ARN of each of its policies on its Permissions tab instead.
  • The last command prints the ARN of each managed policy on the role.
  • An ARN that starts with arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ is AWS managed and takes no tag from you.
  • Any other ARN is a customer managed policy, so tag it too with the command below, pasting that ARN in.
aws iam tag-policy --profile ccp-admin --policy-arn "paste-the-policy-arn-here" --tags Key=ccp:mission,Value=mission-06

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • In the CloudWatch console, open Alarms, choose ccp-m06-errors, and check that its History tab lists a state change to ALARM after your test.
  • Check your inbox for an email about ccp-m06-errors that the topic sent when the alarm changed state.
  • Once later minutes pass with no errors, the alarm reads OK again with no action from you, because those empty minutes count as not breaching.
  • If no email came, check your spam folder and that the subscription reads Confirmed.

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.html:
Cleanup

  • Delete the alarm with aws cloudwatch delete-alarms --profile ccp-admin --alarm-names ccp-m06-errors.
  • Delete the SNS email subscription: in the SNS console, choose Subscriptions, select the confirmed subscription, choose Delete, and confirm.
  • Delete the topic: choose Topics, select ccp-m06-alarm, choose Delete, and type delete me to confirm, since SNS advises removing subscriptions before their topic.
  • Delete the function: in the Lambda console, select ccp-m06-fail, choose Actions, then Delete, and type confirm.
  • Delete the /aws/lambda/<function> log group, which here is /aws/lambda/ccp-m06-fail: in the CloudWatch console under Log groups, select it and choose Actions, then Delete log group(s), because it is a separate resource from the function.
  • Delete the execution role and its policy: open the role in the IAM console, note the policy on its Permissions tab, then delete the role by typing its name, and also delete that policy under Policies if it is the customer managed one you tagged, since an AWS managed one such as AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole stays.
  • Open Tag Editor, choose all Regions and all resource types, search for the tag key ccp:mission, and check that it returns 0 results; delete anything it still lists and search again.

sections.title: Usage check
sections.html:
Usage check

  • On the next study day, open Cost Explorer with daily granularity, grouped by Service.
  • Compare Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon SNS and AWS Lambda with the day before Start, not with zero, and check that each is back to that day's level.
  • Then note the remaining credit balance, which this page records with the usage button.

sections.title: Never do
sections.html:
Never do

  • Never upgrade the account to the Paid plan, and never change the Support plan.
  • Never enable IAM Identity Center or create or join an AWS organization, because on a free-plan account creating an organization upgrades it to the Paid plan and the credits expire at once.
  • Never create a landing zone in AWS Control Tower, join the AWS Partner Network, sign a Professional Services contract or an Enterprise Agreement, or buy an AWS Skill Builder Team subscription, because each of these upgrades a free-plan account too.
  • Never accept an agreement in AWS Artifact, such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA), because marking the account as HIPAA or SEC compliant also upgrades it.
  • Never create access keys, for the root user or for ccp-admin, because aws login gives the CLI short-term credentials.
  • Never create NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses or unattached Elastic IPs.
  • Never create RDS or Aurora databases, EKS clusters, Redshift, OpenSearch or SageMaker endpoints.
  • Never turn on Shield Advanced or order Direct Connect.
  • Never register Route 53 domains or create hosted zones.
  • Never buy Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and never subscribe to Marketplace products.
  • Never give the alarm a period of 10, 20 or 30 seconds, because that makes it a high-resolution alarm, which the free alarm allowance leaves out.
  • Never create a second alarm, a composite alarm, a dashboard, a second topic or a second subscription, and never subscribe anything but your own email address.
  • Never give the alarm any action but the topic, never save a shareable test event, and never invoke the function in a loop or on a schedule.

missions.title: A two-tier VPC with no NAT gateway

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Build the classic two-tier network by hand: one public subnet that reaches the internet through an internet gateway, and one private subnet that has no way out. Put a web security group in front that takes ports 80 and 443 from anywhere, and an app security group that only the web group can reach. Nothing runs inside the network, so you study the routes and the rules themselves, and then you delete all of it.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds.
  • Your Plan status form says the free plan offers Amazon VPC; if it is unticked, stop here.
  • Sign in to the console as ccp-admin, never as the root user, and keep the Region selector on the home Region you picked in Mission 0.
  • Run every CLI command with --profile ccp-admin, and run aws login --profile ccp-admin first if the session has expired.
  • Tag every resource that takes tags with the key ccp:mission and the value mission-07, written ccp:mission=mission-07 on this page.
  • Nothing here should use credits: a VPC has no additional charge, an internet gateway has no charge, and security groups have no additional charge.
  • The parts of Amazon VPC that do bill, such as NAT gateways and public IPv4 addresses, are exactly what this mission's guardrails keep out: no instances, no Elastic IPs, no public IPv4 addresses and no NAT gateway.
  • Write down the time you start, and finish Cleanup within 2 hours of it.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Create the VPC with the wizard

  • In the VPC console, choose Create VPC, then VPC and more under Resources to create.
  • Keep Name tag auto-generation selected and enter ccp-m07, so each piece gets a readable Name tag.
  • Enter 10.0.0.0/16 as the IPv4 CIDR block, add no IPv6 block, and keep Tenancy at Default.
  • The VPC guide lists NAT gateways and the S3 gateway endpoint as optional choices but never says what the form starts with, so before you touch NAT gateways and VPC endpoints, note what each one shows.
  • Then set every field in the table below, even one that already shows that value.
Field Set it to Why
Number of Availability Zones (AZs) 1 One AZ is enough for a test network; production wants two or more
Number of public subnets 1 The web tier
Number of private subnets 1 The app tier
NAT gateways None A NAT gateway bills for every hour and every GB, and a public one needs an Elastic IP
Egress only internet gateway No This network has no IPv6
VPC endpoints None Keep the network to the parts drawn below
DNS options leave as shown Both are on by default and nothing here uses them
  • Expand Additional tags, choose Add new tag, and enter the key ccp:mission with the value mission-07.
  • Read the Preview pane: it should list one VPC, one public and one private subnet and one internet gateway, with no NAT gateway and no endpoint.
  • Choose Create VPC.

Picture the network

                       internet
                          |
                 +------------------+
                 | internet gateway |
                 +------------------+
                          |
+-------------------------|-----------------------------------+
|                         |  VPC ccp-m07, 10.0.0.0/16         |
|                         |                                   |
|  +----------------------+---+    +------------------------+ |
|  | public route table       |    | private route table    | |
|  | 10.0.0.0/16 -> local     |    | 10.0.0.0/16 -> local   | |
|  | 0.0.0.0/0   -> igw-...   |    | (no other route)       | |
|  +------------+-------------+    +-----------+------------+ |
|               | associated                   | associated   |
|  +------------+-------------+    +-----------+------------+ |
|  | public subnet            |    | private subnet         | |
|  | web tier                 |    | app tier               | |
|  +--------------------------+    +------------------------+ |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
  • The wizard gives the public subnet its own route table with a default route to the internet gateway, which is what makes that subnet public.
  • The private subnet has no route to the internet gateway, so even an instance with a public address could not reach the internet from it.
  • Every route table holds the local route for traffic inside the VPC, and a subnet uses exactly one route table at a time.
  • The private subnet may sit on a table the wizard made or on the VPC's main route table; either way that table should list only the local route, and Verify checks it.

Tag what the wizard made

  • The guide documents Additional tags as tagging the VPC, so tag the subnets, route tables and internet gateway as well.
  • Every new VPC also comes with a default security group, named default, and a default network ACL, and both take tags, so tag them too.
  • Run these lines in one terminal and keep it open for Verify.
VPC=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=tag:ccp:mission,Values=mission-07 --query 'Vpcs[0].VpcId' --output text --profile ccp-admin)
echo "$VPC"
SUBNETS=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'Subnets[].SubnetId' --output text --profile ccp-admin)
TABLES=$(aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'RouteTables[].RouteTableId' --output text --profile ccp-admin)
IGW=$(aws ec2 describe-internet-gateways --filters Name=attachment.vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'InternetGateways[].InternetGatewayId' --output text --profile ccp-admin)
SGS=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'SecurityGroups[].GroupId' --output text --profile ccp-admin)
ACLS=$(aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'NetworkAcls[].NetworkAclId' --output text --profile ccp-admin)
aws ec2 create-tags --resources $SUBNETS $TABLES $IGW $SGS $ACLS --tags Key=ccp:mission,Value=mission-07 --profile ccp-admin
  • The echo line prints an ID that starts with vpc-; if it prints None, add the tag on the VPC's Tags tab and run the lines again.

Create the two security groups

  • In the VPC console, choose Security groups, then Create security group.
  • Name it ccp-m07-web, give it a short description, and choose the ccp-m07 VPC.
  • Add two inbound rules, HTTP on port 80 and HTTPS on port 443, each with the source 0.0.0.0/0.
  • Leave the single outbound rule that a new group starts with, which lets all outbound traffic out.
  • Choose Add new tag, enter ccp:mission and mission-07, and choose Create security group.
  • Create a second group named ccp-m07-app in the same VPC with one inbound rule: Custom TCP, port 8080, and as the source the sg- ID of ccp-m07-web.
  • Port 8080 stands in for the app's port; one port is enough, so do not open a range.
  • Tag it the same way and create it.
  • A rule whose source is a security group admits traffic from the private addresses of whatever belongs to that group, and it does not copy that group's own rules.
  • A new group admits no inbound traffic until you add a rule, so nothing on the internet can reach ccp-m07-app.

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • In the VPC console, open Your VPCs, select ccp-m07, and open the Resource map tab: it shows the two subnets, the VPC's route tables and one internet gateway, matching your drawing, and no NAT gateway.
  • Under Route tables, select the public subnet's table: its Routes tab lists exactly 10.0.0.0/16 to local and 0.0.0.0/0 to an ID that starts with igw-.
  • That table's Subnet associations tab lists the public subnet and no other.
  • Select the private subnet's table: its Routes tab lists only 10.0.0.0/16 to local, and its Subnet associations tab lists the private subnet, either as an explicit association or as a subnet without one.
  • Under Subnets, the public subnet shows Auto-assign public IPv4 address as No; if it shows Yes, turn it off with Edit subnet settings.
  • Under Security groups, ccp-m07-web shows inbound 80 and 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and ccp-m07-app shows one inbound rule whose source is the sg- ID of ccp-m07-web.
  • In the terminal from the tagging step, each of these three commands prints []: no network interface in the VPC, so no public IPv4 address, no NAT gateway, and no Elastic IP.
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC --query 'NetworkInterfaces[].NetworkInterfaceId' --output json --profile ccp-admin
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --query 'NatGateways[].NatGatewayId' --output json --profile ccp-admin
aws ec2 describe-addresses --query 'Addresses[].PublicIp' --output json --profile ccp-admin

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.html:
Cleanup

  • This mission lists no leftovers in its frontmatter, so nothing has to go first.
  • In the VPC console, open Your VPCs, select ccp-m07, and choose Actions, Delete VPC.
  • The VPC guide says that a console delete also removes the VPC's subnets, route tables, internet gateways, security groups, network ACLs, gateway endpoints, egress-only internet gateways and DHCP options, so both security groups and the internet gateway go with it.
  • If the console instead lists something you must remove first, such as an instance or a NAT gateway, a guardrail slipped: delete that, then try again.
  • Type delete in the confirmation box and choose Delete.
  • Check that the VPC is gone: aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=tag:ccp:mission,Values=mission-07 --query 'Vpcs[].VpcId' --output json --profile ccp-admin prints [].
  • In Tag Editor, choose all Regions and All resource types, enter the tag key ccp:mission, and choose Search resources: the search returns 0 results.

sections.title: Usage check
sections.html:
Usage check

  • On the next study day, open Cost Explorer with Daily granularity, grouped by Service.
  • Compare Amazon VPC on the day after Start with the day before Start, not with zero: the two match.
  • If Amazon VPC went up, look for a NAT gateway or a public IPv4 address that outlived Cleanup, delete it, and repeat the Tag Editor search.
  • Note your remaining credit balance and record it with the usage button on this page.

sections.title: Never do
sections.html:
Never do

  • Never upgrade the account to the Paid plan, and never change the Support plan.
  • Never create NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses or unattached Elastic IPs; here that means NAT gateways stays at None in the wizard.
  • Never launch an instance into either subnet, and never turn on auto-assign public IPv4 for the public subnet.
  • Never add a VPC endpoint in this mission, and never open ccp-m07-app to 0.0.0.0/0 or add SSH or RDP rules from anywhere.
  • Never create RDS or Aurora databases, EKS clusters, Redshift, OpenSearch or SageMaker endpoints.
  • Never turn on Shield Advanced or order Direct Connect.
  • Never register Route 53 domains or create hosted zones.
  • Never buy Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and never subscribe to Marketplace products.
  • Never create access keys, for the root user or for ccp-admin, because aws login hands the CLI temporary credentials instead.
  • Never enable IAM Identity Center or create or join an AWS organization, because on a free-plan account creating an organization upgrades it to the Paid plan and its credits expire at once.
  • Never create a landing zone in AWS Control Tower, join the AWS Partner Network, accept an agreement in AWS Artifact such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA), sign a Professional Services contract or an Enterprise Agreement, or buy an AWS Skill Builder Team subscription, because each of these upgrades a free-plan account to the Paid plan.

missions.title: Estimate and review the cafe plan

sections.title: Goal
sections.html:
Goal

Put a price on the cafe plan you wrote in the capstone, and hold one part of it up against the AWS Well-Architected Framework. You save a public AWS Pricing Calculator estimate, paste its link into decision 11's Cost note on the Project screen, and answer one pillar's questions about the cafe in the AWS Well-Architected Tool.

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
Before you start

  • Mission 0 is done and its Verify holds.
  • Your Plan status form says the free plan offers AWS Pricing Calculator and the AWS Well-Architected Tool; if either is unticked, stop here.
  • The public Pricing Calculator at https://calculator.aws/ works without an AWS account, so that half of the mission needs no sign-in at all.
  • For the Well-Architected Tool, sign in to the console as ccp-admin, never as the root user, and keep the console on the home Region you chose in Mission 0.
  • Run every CLI command with --profile ccp-admin, after aws login --profile ccp-admin if your session has expired.
  • Tag every taggable resource with the key ccp:mission and the value mission-08, written as ccp:mission=mission-08 in this page; here that is only the workload.
  • Nothing in this mission can use credits: the public Pricing Calculator is a free tool, and AWS offers the Well-Architected Tool at no charge.
  • The free plan charges nothing unless you upgrade to the Paid plan, and it closes the account after 6 months or when the credits run out, whichever comes first.
  • Clean up within 2 hours of Start, as with every mission that is not kept.
  • Capstone decisions open after the exam, so start this mission then, when you can paste the link into decision 11 straight away.
  • Have your capstone decisions 2 to 7 open, because the estimate prices what they chose.

sections.title: Steps
sections.html:
Steps

Build the estimate

  • Open https://calculator.aws/ in a private browser window and choose Create estimate.
  • Add one service for each piece your decisions picked, such as the ordering compute, the receipt and photo storage, the loyalty database and any edge delivery.
  • For each service, write a short description, pick the Region your decisions use, and size it from the brief: the 07:00 to 09:00 rush at 10 times the baseline, 2 TB of receipts and photos, and the shops you plan for.
  • If your decisions chose a Support plan, add it to the estimate as well, because the calculator can price Support plans next to services.
  • Put the services in groups that match your decisions if that makes the summary easier to read.
  • Check the monthly total against the brief's cap of $300 a month, and remember the figure leaves out any taxes.
  • Write descriptions that hold no account IDs, email addresses, names or keys, because the next step publishes them.

Save the estimate and paste its link

  • On the My Estimate page, choose Share, accept the public server notice, and copy the public link.
  • AWS stores the estimate on its public servers, so anyone with the link can open it.
  • Keep the link safe: it is the only way back to the estimate, and a link made today stays valid for one year.
  • An edit to the estimate does not change the saved link, so after any change share again and use the new link.
  • In this site, open the Project screen, open decision 11, and paste the link into its Cost note with one line on the monthly total, such as About $180 a month: https://calculator.aws/#/estimate?id=....

Define the cafe workload

  • In the console, open the AWS Well-Architected Tool, choose Workloads, then Define workload.
  • Name it cafe-cloud-plan, give a short description of the cafe move, and enter yourself as the review owner.
  • Choose Pre-production as the environment, and under AWS Regions choose your home Region.
  • Leave the account IDs, the application, Trusted Advisor and Jira settings empty or off.
  • Under Tags, add the key ccp:mission with the value mission-08, because Tag Editor cannot add tags to a workload for you.
  • Choose Next, skip the profile, and keep the lens list as it is: the AWS Well-Architected Framework Lens is applied to every new workload on its own.
  • Choose Define workload.

Answer one pillar

  • The framework has six pillars: security, cost optimization, reliability, sustainability, operational excellence and performance efficiency.
  • Choose Start reviewing, which opens the first question of the review.
  • The left pane lists the questions under each pillar, so choose Cost optimization there and then its first question, because that pillar matches the estimate you just built.
  • For each question in that pillar, tick the best practices your plan follows, choose None of these when it follows none, or mark the question as not applying to the cafe.
  • Use Info for help, and use Notes to say which capstone decision backs your answer, with no secrets in it.
  • Choose Save and exit when that pillar is done; the other pillars can stay unanswered.
  • The tool turns your answers into high and medium risk issues, which the Workloads list counts for each workload.
  • On the workload page, open the AWS Well-Architected Framework lens, choose Improvement plan, and filter it to the Cost optimization pillar.
  • Copy its high and medium risk items into decision 13 on the Project screen as candidates for your top 3 fixes.

sections.title: Verify
sections.html:
Verify

  • Open the saved link in a private browser window: it starts with https://calculator.aws/ and shows your estimate and its monthly total.
  • On the Project screen, the Cost note of decision 11 holds that link, and the Verify button on this page waits until it finds a https://calculator.aws/ link there.
  • Capstone decisions open after the exam, so this Verify cannot pass before then either.
  • The command below prints cafe-cloud-plan among your workloads.
aws wellarchitected list-workloads --profile ccp-admin --query "WorkloadSummaries[].WorkloadName" --output json
  • The workload's page shows answered questions under the pillar you chose.

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.html:
Cleanup

  • Delete the Well-Architected Tool workload: in the Well-Architected Tool, choose Workloads, select cafe-cloud-plan, choose Delete, and confirm.
  • Deleting a workload removes its answers and any milestones for good, and it cannot be undone, so copy anything you want into decision 13 first.
  • Run the command from Verify again and check that cafe-cloud-plan is no longer in its output; other workloads may still be listed.
  • Keep the estimate link, because it lives in decision 11 and is not an AWS resource in your account.
  • Tag Editor does not list Well-Architected Tool workloads, so the command above is the proof that the workload is gone; the sweep below catches anything else left from earlier missions.
  • In Tag Editor, select every Region and All resource types, search for the tag key ccp:mission, and check that the search returns 0 results.

sections.title: Usage check
sections.html:
Usage check

  • On the next study day, open Cost Explorer with Daily granularity, grouped by Service.
  • Compare each of this mission's services, AWS Pricing Calculator and AWS Well-Architected Tool, with the day before Start, not with zero, and expect no change for either, since both are free.
  • Cost Explorer counts days in UTC, so pick the days around Start with that in mind.
  • Note the remaining credit balance from the Billing and Cost Management console home, and record it on this page with the usage button.

sections.title: Never do
sections.html:
Never do

  • Never upgrade the account to the Paid plan, and never change the Support plan; the Support plan line lives only in the estimate.
  • Never use the in-console Pricing Calculator in Billing and Cost Management for this mission, because its bill estimates cost $2 each after the first five in a month; the public calculator is enough.
  • Never put account IDs, email addresses, passwords or keys in an estimate or in workload notes, because a shared estimate link is public.
  • Never turn on Trusted Advisor or Jira sync for the workload, and never share it with another account.
  • Never enable IAM Identity Center or create or join an AWS organization: on a free-plan account, creating an organization, which enabling IAM Identity Center does, moves the account to the Paid plan and its credits expire at once, and joining one also upgrades it.
  • Never create an AWS Control Tower landing zone or become part of the AWS Partner Network, because either one also moves a free-plan account to the Paid plan.
  • Never accept an agreement in AWS Artifact, such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA), because designating the account as HIPAA or SEC compliant also upgrades a free-plan account to the Paid plan.
  • Never sign a Professional Services contract or an Enterprise Agreement with AWS, or buy an AWS Skill Builder Team subscription, on this account, because each of these upgrades it too.
  • Never create access keys, for the root user or for ccp-admin, because aws login hands the CLI temporary credentials that it refreshes on its own.
  • Never create NAT gateways, idle public IPv4 addresses or unattached Elastic IPs.
  • Never create RDS or Aurora databases, EKS clusters, Redshift, OpenSearch or SageMaker endpoints.
  • Never turn on Shield Advanced or order Direct Connect.
  • Never register Route 53 domains or create hosted zones.
  • Never buy Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, and never subscribe to Marketplace products.

ranks.name: Business Support+
facts: AWS calls Business Support+ the minimum plan it recommends for production workloads.
With Business Support+, a business-critical or mission-critical system that is down gets a response in under 30 minutes.

ranks.name: Enterprise
facts: Enterprise Support includes a designated technical account manager.
With Enterprise Support, a business-critical or mission-critical system that is down gets a response in under 15 minutes.

ranks.name: Unified Operations
facts: Unified Operations is the only plan that includes 24/7 workload monitoring.
With Unified Operations, an Incident Management Engineer responds in under 5 minutes when a business-critical or mission-critical system is down.
